text: Angela Isadora Duncan (May 26, 1877, or May 27, 1878[a] – September 14, 1927) was an American-born dancer and choreographer, a pioneer of modern contemporary dance, who performed to great acclaim throughout Europe and the United States. Born and raised in California, she lived and danced in Western Europe, the U.S., and Soviet Russia from the age of 22. She died when her scarf became entangled in the wheel and axle of the car in which she was traveling in Nice, France.[2] Duncan was born in San Francisco, the youngest of four children, to Joseph Charles Duncan (1819–1898), a banker, mining engineer, and arts connoisseur, and Mary Isadora Gray (1849–1922). Her brothers were Augustin Duncan and Raymond Duncan; her sister, Elizabeth Duncan, was also a dancer.[4][5] Shortly after her birth, her father was investigated and charged[clarification needed] following the collapse of the family’s bank, coinciding with a broader financial crisis in San Francisco and the closing of silver mines.[6] Although acquitted by the jury,[6] her mother divorced him due to his infidelities and the financial scandal, and the family subsequently faced poverty.[3] Joseph Duncan, along with his third wife and their daughter, died in 1898 when the British passenger steamer SS Mohegan ran aground off the coast of Cornwall.[7] After the divorce,[8] Isadora’s mother moved the family to Oakland, California, where she worked as a seamstress and piano teacher. Isadora attended school from ages six to ten but dropped out, finding it constricting. She and her siblings taught dance to local children.[3] In 1896, Duncan joined Augustin Daly’s theater company in New York, but soon became disillusioned with its rigid structure and hierarchy.[9] Her early teaching experiences, where she "followed [her] fantasy and improvised, teaching any pretty thing that came into [her] head," revealed her novel approach to dance.[10] A desire to travel led her to Chicago, where she auditioned for theater companies and eventually joined Daly’s company in New York, where her unique vision clashed with popular pantomimes.[11] While there, she took classes with Marie Bonfanti but quickly became disappointed with ballet routines. Feeling unhappy and unappreciated in America, she moved to London in 1898, performing in wealthy drawing rooms and drawing inspiration from Greek vases and bas-reliefs in the British Museum.[12][13] Earnings from these performances allowed her to rent a studio to develop her work and create larger stage productions.[14] From London, she traveled to Paris, where she was inspired by the Louvre and the Exposition Universelle of 1900 and danced in the salons of Marguerite de Saint-Marceaux and Princesse Edmond de Polignac.[15] In France, as elsewhere, she delighted her audiences.[16] In 1902, Loie Fuller invited her to tour Europe, where she created new works using her innovative technique, emphasizing natural movement in contrast to traditional ballet’s rigidity.[17][18] She spent most of the rest of her life touring Europe and the Americas in this manner.[19] Despite mixed critical reactions, she gained popularity for her distinctive style and inspired visual artists such as Antoine Bourdelle, Dame Laura Knight, Auguste Rodin, Arnold Rönnebeck, André Dunoyer de Segonzac, and Abraham Walkowitz.[20] In 1910, she met the occultist Aleister Crowley at a party, an episode recounted in his Confessions.[21] He referred to her as "Lavinia King" and used that name in his 1929 novel Moonchild (written in 1917), writing that she "has this gift of gesture in a very high degree" and possessed "superb 'unconsciousness' – which is magical consciousness – with which she suits the action to the melody."[22] Crowley was more attracted to Duncan’s companion Mary Dempsey (a.k.a. Mary D'Este or Desti), with whom he had an affair. Desti, who arrived in Paris in 1901 and became inseparable from Duncan, later wrote a memoir of her experiences.[23] In 1911, French fashion designer Paul Poiret rented a mansion – Pavillon du Butard in La Celle-Saint-Cloud – and hosted lavish parties, including La fête de Bacchus on June 20, 1912, re-creating Louis XIV’s Versailles Bacchanalia. Isadora Duncan, wearing a Greek evening gown designed by Poiret,[24] danced on tables among 300 guests; 900 bottles of champagne were consumed until the first light of day.[24] Duncan disliked the commercial aspects of public performance, such as touring and contracts, because she believed they distracted her from her mission of creating beauty and educating young people.[citation needed] To fulfill this mission, she opened schools to teach young girls her philosophy of dance. The first was established in 1904 in Grunewald, Berlin, Germany, and lasted three years. This institution gave rise to the "Isadorables" (Anna, Maria-Theresa,[25][26] Irma, (Gretel),[27][28] Lisa, and Erika[29][30]), whom Duncan optimistically hoped would train “thousands of young dancing maidens” in non-professional community dance.[31] It was a boarding school offering a regular education and dance instruction, but students were not expected or encouraged to become professional dancers.[32] Duncan did not legally adopt all six girls, as commonly believed.[33] However, three of them (Irma,[34] Anna[35] and Lisa[36][37]) used the Duncan surname for life.[38][39] After about a decade in Berlin, she established a school in Paris that closed due to the outbreak of World War I.[40] In 1914, Duncan moved to the United States and transferred her school there, using a townhouse on Gramercy Park in New York and a studio on the northeast corner of 23rd Street and Fourth Avenue (now Park Avenue South).[41] Otto Kahn, head of Kuhn, Loeb & Co., provided her with use of the modern Century Theatre at West 60th Street and Central Park West for performances, including a staging of Oedipus Rex involving her extended entourage and friends.[42] During her time in New York, she posed for studies by photographer Arnold Genthe. Duncan had planned to leave the U.S. in 1915 aboard the RMS Lusitania, but historians believe her financial situation led her to choose a more modest crossing.[43] In 1921, her leftist sympathies brought her to the Soviet Union, where she founded a school in Moscow. However, the Soviet government failed to support her work, leading her to return to the West in 1924 and leave the school to her protégée and adopted daughter, German-born Irma Doretta Henrietta Erih-Grimm Duncan (1897–1977).[44] In 1924, she composed a dance routine called Varshavianka to the tune of the Polish revolutionary song known in English as Whirlwinds of Danger.[45] Breaking with convention, Duncan believed dance originated as a sacred art and developed a style of free, natural movement inspired by classical Greek arts, folk dances, social dances, nature, and natural forces, as well as American athleticism involving skipping, running, jumping, leaping, and tossing.[47][failed verification] She wrote of American dancing: "let them come forth with great strides, leaps and bounds, with lifted forehead and far-spread arms, to dance."[48] Her focus on natural movement emphasized steps outside of codified ballet technique. She cited the sea as an early inspiration for movement and believed movement originated from the solar plexus.[49][50] She emphasized "evolutionary" dance motion, insisting each movement arose from the one before it and gave rise to the next in organic succession. This philosophy and technique earned her the title of the creator of modern dance. Duncan’s philosophy moved away from rigid ballet toward natural movement, and she sought to connect emotions and movement, stating, "I spent long days and nights in the studio seeking that dance which might be the divine expression of the human spirit through the medium of the body's movement."[50] She believed dance should encompass all aspects of life—joy and sadness—and drew inspiration from ancient Greece, combining it with a passion for freedom of movement. This is evident in her revolutionary costume of a white Greek tunic and bare feet, which allowed greater freedom than corseted ballet costumes and pointe shoes.[51] She also drew inspiration from ancient Greek art, using some of its forms in her movement (as shown in photos).[52] Duncan bore three children out of wedlock: Deirdre Beatrice, born September 24, 1906, whose father was theatre designer Gordon Craig; Patrick Augustus, born May 1, 1910, fathered by Paris Singer, a son of sewing machine magnate Isaac Singer; both died by drowning in 1913 while on a car ride with their nanny, when the automobile accidentally went into the River Seine.[53] Following this tragedy, she spent time on the Greek island of Corfu with her brother and sister, and later at the Viareggio seaside resort in Italy with actress Eleonora Duse. In her autobiography, Duncan described, in deep despair over her children’s deaths, begging a young Italian sculptor, Romano Romanelli, to sleep with her for a child.[54] She gave birth to a son on August 13, 1914, who died shortly after birth.[55][56] During her stay at Viareggio with Duse, who had recently ended a relationship with the rebellious feminist Lina Poletti, speculation arose about the nature of Duncan and Duse’s relationship, though no evidence supports a romantic connection.[57] Duncan was loving and close to her mother, siblings, and all her friends.[57] In 1921, after the Russian Revolution, she moved to Moscow, where she met poet Sergei Yesenin, who was eighteen years her junior. On May 2, 1922, they officially married, and Duncan took Soviet citizenship. Yesenin accompanied her on tours of Europe and the United States, but the marriage was brief as they grew apart. In May 1923, Yesenin returned to Moscow and was found dead in an apparent suicide.[58] She also had a relationship with poet and playwright Mercedes de Acosta, documented in numerous letters between them.[59] In one, Duncan wrote, "Mercedes, lead me with your little strong hands and I will follow you – to the top of a mountain. To the end of the world. Wherever you wish."[60] However, de Acosta’s claim of a posthumous relationship is disputed; friends and relatives believe it is false due to forged letters and publicity motives.[61][62][63][64] Lily Dikovskaya, one of Duncan’s Moscow students, wrote in In Isadora’s Steps that Duncan “was focused on higher things.”[65] By the late 1920s, in her late 40s, Duncan was depressed by the deaths of her three young children. She spent her final years financially struggling, moving between Paris and the Mediterranean and accumulating hotel debts. Her autobiography, My Life, was published in 1927 shortly after her death. The Australian composer Percy Grainger called it a "life-enriching masterpiece."[66] In his book Isadora, An Intimate Portrait, Sewell Stokes described her extravagant waywardness. In a sketch reminiscent of Zelda Fitzgerald, who and her husband F. Scott Fitzgerald once sat in a Paris café watching a somewhat drunken Duncan, he recalled that while all eyes were on her, she stole the salt and pepper shakers from the table.[67] On September 14, 1927, in Nice, France, Duncan was a passenger in an Amilcar CGSS automobile owned by Benoît Falchetto, a French-Italian mechanic. She wore a long, flowing, hand-painted silk scarf, created by Russian-born artist Roman Chatov, a gift from her friend Mary Desti, the mother of American filmmaker Preston Sturges. Desti, who saw her off, had asked her to wear a cape for the cold weather, but she agreed to wear only the scarf.[68] As they departed, she reportedly said to Desti and companions, "Adieu, mes amis. Je vais à la gloire!" ("Farewell, my friends. I go to glory!"); however, according to American novelist Glenway Wescott, Desti later told him the actual words were "Je vais à l'amour" ("I am off to love"), which Desti considered embarrassing as it suggested a tryst with Falchetto.[69][70][71] Her silk scarf, draped around her neck, became entangled in the wheel well of the open-spoked wheels and rear axle, pulling her from the car and breaking her neck.[2] Desti called out to warn her almost immediately after the car left and took her to the hospital, where she was pronounced dead.[68] The New York Times noted in its obituary that Duncan "met a tragic death at Nice on the Riviera," stating that she was "hurled in an extraordinary manner from an open automobile in which she was riding and instantly killed by the force of her fall onto the stone pavement."[72] Other sources noted she was almost decapitated by the sudden tightening of the scarf around her neck.[73] The accident led Gertrude Stein to remark that "affectations can be dangerous."[74] At the time of her death, Duncan was a Soviet citizen. Her will was the first of a Soviet citizen to undergo probate in the U.S.[75] She was cremated, and her ashes were placed next to those of her children[76] in the columbarium at Père Lachaise Cemetery in Paris.[77] On her headstone is inscribed École du Ballet de l'Opéra de Paris ("Ballet School of the Opera of Paris"). Duncan is known as "The Mother of Dance." Though her schools in Europe did not last long, her work had a lasting impact, and her style is still danced based on the instruction of Maria-Theresa Duncan,[78] Anna Duncan,[79] and Irma Duncan,[80] three of her six pupils. Through her sister, Elizabeth, her approach was adopted by Jarmila Jeřábková from Prague, where her legacy persists.[81] By 1913, she was already celebrated; when the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées was built, her likeness was carved in its bas-relief over the entrance by sculptor Antoine Bourdelle and included in painted murals of the nine muses by Maurice Denis in the auditorium. In 1987, she was inducted into the National Museum of Dance and Hall of Fame. Anna, Lisa,[82] Theresa, and Irma, pupils of her first school, carried on her aesthetic and pedagogical principles in New York and Paris. Choreographer and dancer Julia Levien was instrumental in advancing Duncan’s work through the formation of the Duncan Dance Guild in the 1950s and the establishment of the Duncan Centenary Company in 1977.[83] Another means of preserving her techniques was through the formation of the Isadora Duncan Heritage Society by Mignon Garland, who had been taught by two of Duncan’s key students. Garland was a devoted fan who later lived in a building at the same site and address as Duncan, attached a commemorative plaque near the entrance, which remains as of 2016[update]. Garland also succeeded in having San Francisco rename an alley on the same block from Adelaide Place to Isadora Duncan Lane.[84][85] In medicine, the Isadora Duncan Syndrome refers to injury or death.

Anna, Lisa, Theresa, and Irma, who were pupils of Isadora Duncan's first school, continued the aesthetic and pedagogical principles of Isadora's work in New York and Paris. Choreographer and dancer Julia Levien played a key role in advancing Duncan's legacy by founding the Duncan Dance Guild in the 1950s and establishing the Duncan Centenary Company in 1977. Another way Duncan's dance techniques were preserved was through the formation of the Isadora Duncan Heritage Society by Mignon Garland, who had been taught by two of Duncan's key students. Garland, a devoted admirer, later resided in a building at the same site and address as Duncan and attached a commemorative plaque near the entrance, which remains in place as of 2016. She also successfully lobbied for San Francisco to rename an alley on the same block from Adelaide Place to Isadora Duncan Lane. In medicine, the Isadora Duncan Syndrome refers to injury or death resulting from entanglement of neckwear with a wheel or other machinery. Duncan has drawn literary and artistic attention from the 1920s to the present, appearing in novels, film, ballet, theatre, music, and poetry. In literature, Duncan is portrayed in various works.
